questions.q: What is the main difference between `docker pull` and `docker run`?
options: docker run cannot download images at all
docker pull downloads an image without creating or starting a container from it; docker run will pull automatically but also creates and starts a container
docker pull only works on Windows
They are two names for exactly the same command
questions.explain: `docker pull` just fetches the image. `docker run` pulls the image if it's missing, then goes further and creates and starts a container from it.

questions.q: Why might Northbridge's production deploys pin an image by digest instead of by tag?
options: A tag like node:20 can be repointed to different content later; a digest is a fixed hash of exact content that never changes
Digests download faster than tags
Tags are not supported in production environments
Digests are required for any image over 1GB
questions.explain: A tag is a movable label -- the same tag can point to different bytes over time. A digest is a SHA-256 hash of the exact content, so pinning to it guarantees the same image every time.

questions.q: In `docker run -d --name catalog -p 8080:3000 -e NODE_ENV=production northbridge/catalog:1.4`, what does `-p 8080:3000` do?
options: Sets two environment variables
Limits the container to 8080 megabytes of memory and 3000 CPU shares
Maps host port 8080 to the container's port 3000, so the app is reachable at localhost:8080
Pulls version 8080.3000 of the image
questions.explain: The `-p host:container` flag publishes a container port to a port on the host machine, in the form host-port:container-port.

questions.q: What does the `-d` flag do in a `docker run` command?
options: Downloads the image twice to verify integrity
Deletes the container immediately after it exits
Enables debug logging for the container
Runs the container in the background (detached) and returns control of the shell
questions.explain: `-d` (detached) starts the container in the background instead of attaching your terminal to it, so you get the shell prompt back immediately.

questions.q: Before pulling a third-party image from Docker Hub, what should you check?
options: Whether it carries an Official Image or Verified Publisher badge, when it was last updated, and whether a specific version tag is available
Only the number of stars it has received
Nothing -- all images on Docker Hub are equally trustworthy
Whether the image name is shorter than 20 characters
questions.explain: An Official Image or Verified Publisher badge, a recent update date, and a pinned version tag (rather than relying on :latest) are the signals worth checking before trusting an image.
